subtopics.example: A school finds that a former teacher's account was still active and was used to view grades. Ben, a technician, sorts the fixes by function: disabling the account is corrective, automatic removal when staff leave is preventive, and a monthly inactive-account report is detective. Ben logs each fix as a ticket.

review: Label each control by both type and function
Identify risks covered only by detection
evidence: Control inventory listing type and function
Incident records showing caught or missed events
audit_focus.recommend: Share function gaps with the security manager, highest risks first.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which gaps to close first

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask what the control does when the threat arrives: stop, notice, fix, discourage, restore or stand in.

exam_traps.trap: Warning signs are preventive controls.
exam_traps.why: A sign only discourages, so it is a deterrent. Preventive controls block the action, like a lock.

key_terms.definition: How a control is carried out: technical, administrative or physical.
A control that tells people what to do, such as a policy.

subtopics.name: Layering and Compensating Controls
subtopics.definition: Layering means protecting an asset with several controls of different types and functions, so when one fails, others still protect it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every control can fail. Mixing types means one mistake does not lead straight to a breach.
how_it_works: Cover each important risk with several types: a policy, a technical block, a physical lock.
Mix functions, so failed prevention is still detected and corrected; 4.2 covers network defense in depth.
When a required control is impossible, a compensating control reduces the same risk another way.
It is approved as a recorded, time-limited exception and reviewed.
subtopics.example: A food bank's payroll system already requires multifactor authentication (MFA), as its access standard says. After phishing hits nearby charities, Ade, a security analyst, proposes alerts for sign-ins from new countries and a monthly review of bank-detail changes. Nothing required is missing, so no exception is needed; Ade submits the added detective layers as a normal change for the system owner's approval.

review: Test each substitute against the threat it stands in for
Record each exception with its approver and review date
evidence: Exception record listing the missing control and substitutes
Alarm tests or log reviews showing substitutes work
audit_focus.recommend: Document missing controls and proposed substitutes for the rule owner's approval.
audit_focus.decides: The owner of the policy or standard approves the exception; the risk owner accepts what remains

subtopics.isaca_rule: Never rely on one control. When the usual one cannot be used, add compensating controls through the exception process.

exam_traps.trap: If the required control cannot be installed, accept the risk and move on.
exam_traps.why: First look for compensating controls. Any acceptance belongs to the risk owner, not the practitioner.

exam_traps.trap: Adding more controls of the same kind gives layered protection.
exam_traps.why: Two firewalls with the same rules fail the same way. Real layering mixes types and functions.

key_terms.definition: Layering independent controls so one failure does not expose the asset.
A scheduled check that an exception is still needed and its substitutes still work.

subtopics.name: Controls for AI Tools
subtopics.definition: AI tools need the same three control types as any system: technical, administrative and physical safeguards for their data, models and actions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI systems handle sensitive data and act automatically, so one gap can let a poisoned or tricked model cause harm at scale.
how_it_works: Technical: limit who can change models and training data, filter inputs and outputs, and log prompts with the model version used.
Administrative: an AI use policy, a risk review before launch and human review of high-impact outputs.
Physical: secure the hardware that holds models and training data.
AI agents get least-privilege accounts, so a manipulated agent can do only limited harm.
subtopics.example: A bookshop chain's AI agent reorders stock from publishers. Sana, a security analyst, finds its service account can also change suppliers' bank details. Sana sorts fixes by type: an account limited to placing orders (technical), a spending cap in the purchasing policy (administrative) and a locked server cabinet (physical), and sends the account change to the system owner for approval.

review: Confirm the AI agent's permissions cover only its task
Log prompts, outputs and model versions for AI tools you run
evidence: Permission list for the AI service account
Log entries tying each AI output to its prompt, model version and approver
audit_focus.recommend: Report AI tools lacking logging or human review to the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts remaining risk before deployment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Classify AI controls like any others. Keep a person accountable for high-impact AI decisions, and limit and log what AI agents can do.

exam_traps.trap: AI tools need only technical controls because they are software.
exam_traps.why: They also need policy, human review and physical protection of their hardware.

exam_traps.trap: Human review is unnecessary once a model tests as accurate.
exam_traps.why: Models drift, get poisoned or are tricked by crafted input. Human review catches what testing missed.

key_terms.definition: A person reviews or approves an AI system's output before it takes effect.
A non-human account a program or AI agent uses; 3.1 covers its life cycle.

topics.overview: This topic covers how a security professional is expected to behave: following a code of conduct, showing due care and due diligence, and living by the ISC2 Code of Ethics. It also covers reasoning through ethical dilemmas, how the code is enforced, and ethical use of AI at work.
can_do: Tell due care from due diligence in a scenario
State the four ISC2 canons in their listed order and apply all of them to a dilemma
Choose the action that protects the public while staying honest and legal
Identify who may file an ethics complaint under each canon

subtopics.name: Professional Code of Conduct
subtopics.definition: A professional code of conduct is a written set of expected behaviors, from an employer or professional body, covering honesty, conflicts of interest and confidentiality.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security staff hold powerful access. A code makes expectations clear and gives a basis for action when someone crosses the line.
how_it_works: Employers publish codes of conduct that staff accept, often with the acceptable use policy.
Professional bodies, such as ISC2, have codes members must follow to keep their certification.
Common themes are honesty, avoiding conflicts of interest and protecting confidential information.
When a personal link could sway your judgment, disclose it to your manager before you start, and let them decide whether to reassign the work.
Use access only for assigned work, and raise concerns through proper channels.
subtopics.example: Coworkers at a hospital ask Nia, a database administrator, to look up the diagnosis of a well-known local figure who has just been admitted. Nia refuses, because the access exists only for assigned work, and reports the request to the privacy officer, as the hospital's code of conduct requires.

review: Check new work for personal ties to vendors, candidates or cases
Confirm a ticket or task needs a record before you open it
evidence: Signed code of conduct and acceptable use acknowledgment
Conflict-of-interest declarations on file with your manager
audit_focus.recommend: Report requests to misuse access to your manager, the privacy officer or the ethics hotline.
audit_focus.decides: Your manager decides how a declared conflict is handled

subtopics.isaca_rule: Access is a trust, not a perk. Use it only for assigned work, avoid conflicts of interest, keep confidences and raise concerns through proper channels.

exam_traps.trap: Looking at records out of curiosity is harmless if you change nothing.
exam_traps.why: Having access is not having a reason. Viewing records without a work need breaches confidentiality and the code.

exam_traps.trap: A professional body's code replaces the employer's code of conduct.
exam_traps.why: Both apply. Raise any conflict between them instead of silently picking one.

key_terms.definition: When personal interests could sway professional decisions, such as assessing a vendor you own shares in.
A channel, often anonymous, for reporting suspected misconduct outside your direct manager.

subtopics.name: Due Care and Due Diligence
subtopics.definition: Due diligence is investigating risks and checking that safeguards work; due care is acting on that knowledge as a prudent person would.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Courts, regulators and customers judge whether an organization acted reasonably. Falling short on either can count as negligence.
how_it_works: Due diligence investigates: researching a vendor, assessing risks, testing controls.
Due care acts: patching known flaws, enforcing policy, fixing what diligence found.
Both are ongoing: diligence keeps checking, care keeps acting on the results.
The test is what a reasonable, informed professional would have done, judged by conduct, not by whether an attack still succeeded.

rows.label: Core idea
cells: Do: act responsibly on what you know

rows.label: Example
cells: Reviewing a cloud vendor's security reports before signing
Requiring a second sign-in factor after learning staff are being phished

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: Did we find out what we should have known?
Did we do what a reasonable person would do?

subtopics.example: Before a city council signs with a payroll provider, Grace, a security analyst, reviews the provider's independent security report and finds weak backup practices: due diligence. The council makes tested backups a contract condition: due care. Grace schedules yearly re-checks and records each step in the contract file.

review: Review a vendor's security evidence before the contract is signed
Follow each finding through to a fix or a recorded decision
evidence: Dated vendor security review records
Closed remediation tickets for earlier findings
audit_focus.recommend: Report findings with no follow-up action to their owner as a due care gap.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides the reasonable level of protection

subtopics.isaca_rule: Diligence is finding out; care is acting on what you found. Researching, assessing or verifying is diligence; implementing, enforcing or fixing is care.

exam_traps.trap: Knowing about a risk is enough to show due care.
exam_traps.why: Knowledge without action is what negligence claims target. Care means acting on it.

key_terms.definition: Asking what a reasonable, careful person with similar knowledge would have done.
Failing to take reasonable care, leading to foreseeable harm.

subtopics.memory_aid: Diligence discovers; care carries it out.

subtopics.name: The ISC2 Code of Ethics
subtopics.definition: The ISC2 Code of Ethics is the set of mandatory principles every ISC2-certified member agrees to follow: a preamble and four canons.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Following the code is a condition of certification, and a proven breach can cost the credential.
how_it_works: The preamble explains why the code exists: others rely on members behaving ethically.
The canons below are in ISC2's order, in short form; the exact wording is on ISC2's ethics page.
ISC2 gives no ranking rule; judge conflicts by the facts, protecting people first in safety cases.

types.meaning: Protect society, the common good, the public trust and confidence it depends on, and the infrastructure.
Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally.
Give diligent, competent service to principals, such as employers and clients.

subtopics.example: A friend at a rival firm asks a newly certified analyst for their employer's internal incident response playbook. Handing it over would fail their duty to their employer (canon 3) and be dishonest (canon 2). They decline and suggest free guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).

review: Test a planned action against all four canons, not only the first
Name the principals you serve on each job, such as employer and client
evidence: Your signed agreement to follow the code
Notes of how you raised and settled an ethics concern
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any request that would break a canon with your manager, and refuse illegal or dishonest steps.
audit_focus.decides: The certifying body's board decides sanctions on its ethics committee's advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Learn the four canons in their listed order so you can recall them: the public, honest and legal conduct, principals, and the profession. The order helps memory; it is not a ranking, so in a dilemma check all four (see 1.5.4).

exam_traps.trap: The code is voluntary guidance for good behavior.
exam_traps.why: Following it is a condition of holding ISC2 certification. A proven breach can cost the credential.

exam_traps.trap: Principals means only the company's leadership.
exam_traps.why: Principals are those you serve professionally, such as employers and clients.

key_terms.definition: Anyone a professional serves under an agreement, such as an employer or client.
The opening statement of the code, explaining its purpose.

subtopics.memory_aid: Listed order: society, honor, principals, profession.

subtopics.name: Applying the Canons to Dilemmas
subtopics.definition: Applying the canons means testing each possible action against all four and choosing one that protects the public while staying honest, legal and responsible.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Real dilemmas pit loyalty to an employer against public safety or honesty, and ISC2 gives no ranking rule, so judgment is needed.
how_it_works: List the options; ask of each whether it harms the public, breaks the law or needs dishonesty.
Reject any illegal or deceptive option, even if an employer asks for it.
Where people's safety is at stake, protecting them comes first.
The best option usually satisfies several canons, such as reporting a safety issue through official channels.
Report flaws to the owner first; publishing before a fix hands attackers a way in.
Stay within your authority: test only with the system owner's written permission, whoever is paying, and never hack back.
subtopics.example: A security engineer at a medical device maker finds that an infusion pump's wireless link lets anyone change doses. The engineer's manager says to stay quiet until the next release. The engineer documents the flaw and escalates it to the product security lead and the compliance team, pressing for patient warnings, because silence would leave patients at risk.

review: List each option and ask whether it is honest, legal and safe
Get the system owner's signed scope before any test starts
evidence: Authorization letters naming the systems and dates you may test
Written record of a safety issue you escalated, and to whom
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate safety flaws through official channels to the system owner, and decline deceptive or illegal tasks.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner and management decide fixes and public warnings

subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the action you could defend to the public, a regulator and your employer at once: honest, legal, protective of people and done through proper channels.

exam_traps.trap: Loyalty to the employer means keeping a flaw quiet when told to.
exam_traps.why: Canon 3 asks for diligent service, not concealment that endangers the public or needs dishonesty.

exam_traps.trap: Canon 1 is listed first, so it settles every conflict on its own.
exam_traps.why: ISC2 gives no ranking rule. Judge by the facts: protect people first when safety is at stake, and honor the other canons too.

key_terms.definition: Reporting serious wrongdoing to authorities, often after internal channels fail; many laws protect it.
Attacking an attacker's systems in return; usually illegal and unethical.

subtopics.name: Ethics Complaints and Enforcement
subtopics.definition: ISC2 enforces its code through a formal process: a written, sworn complaint is reviewed by an ethics committee and may lead to sanctions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The process gives the code real consequences and sets out who may complain about which canon.
how_it_works: Complaints are sworn written statements that name the canon broken and include evidence.
Anyone may complain under canons 1 and 2; only principals, such as employers or clients, under canon 3.
Under canon 4, only fellow certified or licensed professionals who follow an ethics code may complain.
The committee does not investigate; it weighs submitted evidence and recommends action to the ISC2 board, which can revoke certification.
Members who see another member breach the code are expected to report it; staying silent may breach canon 4.
subtopics.example: A project manager believes a certified contractor falsely reported finishing a security test. As the client who hired the contractor, the manager has standing under canon 3 as well as canon 2. They write and swear the complaint, name both canons and attach the test records.

review: Identify which canon was broken and whether you may complain
Gather the evidence yourself before filing, since the committee will not investigate
evidence: Signed, sworn statement with the supporting records attached
Reports, emails or test records that show the breach
audit_focus.recommend: File a sworn complaint with the certifying body's ethics committee instead of accusing a colleague publicly.
audit_focus.decides: The certifying body's board decides sanctions on the committee's advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the concern to the canon and to who has standing: anyone for canons 1 and 2, principals for canon 3, fellow professionals for canon 4.

exam_traps.trap: Any member of the public can complain under any canon.
exam_traps.why: Standing depends on the canon. Canon 3 complaints come from principals, canon 4 from fellow professionals.

exam_traps.trap: The ethics committee investigates every rumor about a member.
exam_traps.why: It does not investigate. It reviews sworn complaints and closes those without a solid initial case.

key_terms.definition: The right to bring a complaint, based on your relationship to the matter.
A written statement the writer formally swears is true.

subtopics.name: Ethical Use of AI at Work
subtopics.definition: Ethical AI use means bringing the same honesty, care and respect for people's data to AI tools as to any other work, with a person answerable for results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI makes it easy to leak confidential data, pass off unchecked output or act on wrong answers. The canons still apply.
how_it_works: Keep principals' confidential data out of AI tools not approved for it.
Check AI output before relying on it; competent service means verifying, not pasting.
Be honest about AI's role where it matters, such as in reports.
Never use AI to deceive or impersonate outside an authorized test.
subtopics.example: Tara, a junior analyst at a consulting firm, uses an approved AI assistant to summarize a client's scan results. The summary says a server is fully patched, but the raw data shows a critical patch is missing. Tara corrects the report before sending it and tells the team lead.

review: Confirm a tool is approved for the data before pasting it in
Compare AI summaries with the source data before sending them
evidence: The approved AI tool list and the data each may take
Reports noting where AI was used and who checked it
audit_focus.recommend: Tell your team lead about wrong AI output; report data sent to an unapproved tool to your supervisor and the security team at once.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves AI tools; data owners decide what data each may take

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI is a tool; the professional stays accountable. Protect principals' data, verify output, be honest about how work was produced and stay within your authorization.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI made the mistake, the analyst is not responsible.
exam_traps.why: Whoever relies on the output owns the result. Competent service means checking AI work first.

exam_traps.trap: Using AI to write a convincing phishing email is fine if it is only practice.
exam_traps.why: Attack content is acceptable only inside an authorized, scoped test. Otherwise it risks real harm.

key_terms.definition: AI output that sounds confident but is false or made up.
Security testing done with written permission and an agreed scope from the system's owner.

key_terminologies.CIA triad: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three core goals of security.
key_terminologies.AAA: Authentication, authorization and accounting: prove identity, grant permissions, record activity.
key_terminologies.Non-repudiation: Proof strong enough that a person cannot credibly deny an action, usually from a digital signature.
key_terminologies.Personally identifiable information (PII: Data that identifies a person, alone or combined with other data.
key_terminologies.Privacy by design: Building privacy protections into a system from the first design step, with protective defaults.
key_terminologies.Threat: Anything that could harm an asset, such as an attacker, an error or a storm.
key_terminologies.Vulnerability: A weakness a threat can exploit, such as unpatched software.
key_terminologies.Risk: The likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability, combined with the impact if it does.
key_terminologies.Risk treatment: Responding to a risk by avoiding, mitigating, transferring or accepting it.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk left after controls are applied; its owner may accept it within tolerance, and only senior management can accept it beyond.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The broad amount and type of risk the board and senior management will take on to meet goals.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The narrower, measurable limit of risk accepted for a specific objective.
key_terminologies.Risk owner: The person with authority to decide a risk's treatment and accept what remains within tolerance.
key_terminologies.Annualized loss expectancy (ALE): Expected yearly loss from a risk: single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence.
key_terminologies.Regulation: A mandatory rule issued by a government agency under the authority of a law.
key_terminologies.Framework: A published, usually voluntary structure for building a security program, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0.
key_terminologies.Policy: A mandatory, high-level statement of what is required and why, approved by senior management.
key_terminologies.Standard: A mandatory, specific requirement that supports a policy, such as approved encryption settings.
key_terminologies.Procedure: Mandatory step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task.
key_terminologies.Guideline: Optional, recommended practice that leaves room for judgment.
key_terminologies.Technical control: A safeguard built into hardware or software, such as a firewall or encryption.
key_terminologies.Administrative control: A policy, procedure, training or people practice that directs behavior.
key_terminologies.Physical control: A tangible safeguard for people and facilities, such as a lock, fence or guard.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control that lowers the same risk when the usual control is not possible, approved as a recorded exception.
key_terminologies.Due diligence: Investigating and verifying: finding out what risks exist and whether safeguards work.
key_terminologies.Due care: Acting responsibly on what you know, as a reasonable person would.
key_terminologies.ISC2 Code of Ethics: The preamble and four canons every ISC2-certified member must follow.
key_terminologies.Model or data poisoning: Corrupting an AI model or its training data so it learns wrong or hidden behavior; an integrity attack.
key_terminologies.Malware: Malicious software, such as a virus, worm or ransomware, built to harm systems or steal data.
